title: The days of creation and the borrowed light
source_text: Νῦν δὲ διηγήσασθαι τὸν περὶ νοητῶν καὶ αἰσθητῶν λόγον, καὶ τίνα τρόπον διανενέμηνται αἱ φύσεις τῶν ἡμερῶν εἰς ἀμφότερα τὰ εἴδη, οὐ πρόκειται οὐδὲ τὰ κατὰ τοὺς τόπους ἐξετάσαι· ὅλων γὰρ ἡμῖν συντάξεων χρεία εἰς τὴν διήγησιν τῆς κατὰ Μωϋσέα κοσμοποιΐας· ὅπερ κατὰ τὸ δυνατὸν ἡμῖν πρὸ πλείονος χρόνου τῆς ἐνεστηκυίας πρὸς τὸν Κέλσον συντάξεως πεποιήκαμεν, ἀπὸ τῆς πρὸ πλειόνων ἐτῶν ἕξεως, ἧς ἐχωροῦμεν τότε, διαλαβόντες περὶ τῶν κατὰ Μωϋσέα [τῶν] ἓξ τῆς κοσμοποιΐας ἡμερῶν. εἰδέναι μέντοι γε χρὴ ὅτι τοῖς δικαίοις διὰ τοῦ Ἡσαΐου ὁ λόγος ἐπαγγέλλεται ἐν καταστάσει ἔσεσθαι ἡμέρας, ἐν ᾗ μὴ ἥλιος ἀλλ᾿ αὐτὸς ὁ „κύριος φῶς“ ἔσται αὐτοῖς „αἰώνιον, καὶ ὁ θεὸς δόξα“ αὐτῶν. παρακούσας δ᾿ οἶμαι μοχθηρᾶς αἱρέσεώς τινος καὶ κακῶς διηγησαμένης τὸ „γενηθήτω φῶς“ ὡς εὐκτικῶς ὑπὸ τοῦ δημιουργοῦ εἰρημένον εἶπεν· οὐ γὰρ δὴ καθάπερ οἱ τοὺς λύχνους ἐκ γειτόνων ἐναυόμενοι φῶς ὁ δημιουργὸς ἄνωθεν ἐχρήσατο. καὶ ἄλλης δ᾿ ἀσεβοῦς αἱρέσεως παρακούσας εἶπε καὶ τό· εἰ μὲν ἐναντίος τις ἦν τῷ μεγάλῳ θεῷ θεὸς κατηραμένος ὁ ταῦτα ποιῶν παρὰ γνώμην τὴν ἐκείνου, τί αὐτῷ τὸ φῶς ἐκίχρα; πρὸς ἃ τοσοῦτον ἀποδέομεν ἀπολογεῖσθαι, ὥστε τρανότερον ἡμᾶς ἐθέλειν τῆς ἐκείνων δόξης ὡς ἐσφαλμένων κατηγορεῖν καὶ ἵστασθαι οὐ πρὸς ἃ μὴ οἴδαμεν αὐτῶν ὡς ὁ Κέλσος ἀλλὰ πρὸς ἃ ἀκριβῶς γινώσκομεν, πῇ μὲν ἀπ᾿ αὐτῶν, ἀκολουθήσαντες, πῇ δὲ τοῖς συγγράμμασιν αὐτῶν ἐπιμελῶς ἐντυχόντες.
pass_a_gloss: But now to narrate (διηγέομαι) the account (λόγος) about intelligibles (νοητά) and sensibles (αἰσθητά), and in what manner the natures (φύσεις) of the days have been distributed (διανέμω) into both kinds (εἴδη), is not set before us (οὐ πρόκειται), nor to examine the passages (τόποι); for we would need whole treatises (συντάξεις) for the exposition (διήγησις) of the world-making (κοσμοποιΐα) according to Moses; which, as far as possible, we did a long time before the present treatise against Celsus, from the condition (ἕξις) of many years before, of which we were capable (χωρέω) then, discussing (διαλαμβάνω) the six days of the world-making according to Moses. One must know, however, that to the righteous (δίκαιοι) through Isaiah the word (λόγος) promises (ἐπαγγέλλομαι) [that they] will be in a state (κατάστασις) of day, in which not the sun but the Lord (κύριος) himself will be to them everlasting light (φῶς αἰώνιον), and God their glory (δόξα). Having misheard (παρακούω), I think, some wicked (μοχθηρός) sect (αἵρεσις) that explained badly ‘let there be light’ (γενηθήτω φῶς) as said by the Creator (δημιουργός) in the manner of a wish (εὐκτικῶς), he said: ‘For indeed not like those who kindle (ἐναύω) their lamps from neighbours did the Creator borrow (κίχρημι, middle: ἐχρήσατο) light from above.’ And having misheard another impious (ἀσεβής) sect he said also: ‘If he who made these things against that one’s will (γνώμη) was a god opposed (ἐναντίος) to the great God, accursed (καταράομαι), why did he lend (κίχρημι: ἐκίχρα) him the light?’ To which we are so far from (ἀποδέω) needing to defend ourselves (ἀπολογέομαι) that we wish more plainly (τρανότερον) to accuse (κατηγορέω) their opinion (δόξα) as having erred (σφάλλω), and to stand (ἵσταμαι) not against what of theirs we do not know, as Celsus, but against what we know accurately (ἀκριβῶς γινώσκω), partly from them, having followed (ἀκολουθέω), partly having carefully (ἐπιμελῶς) read (ἐντυγχάνω) their writings (συγγράμματα).
pass_b_english: But it is not our purpose now to give the account of things known by the mind and things perceived by the senses, and of how the natures of the days are divided between both kinds, nor to examine the passages one by one. For we would need whole treatises to explain the creation of the world as Moses tells it. This we did, as far as we could, long before the present treatise against Celsus, when, with the grasp we had many years ago, such as it was then, we discussed the six days of creation in Moses.

One should know, however, that through Isaiah the word promises the righteous that they will be in a state of day, in which not the sun but “the Lord” himself will be to them “an everlasting light, and God” their “glory” (Isaiah 60:19).

It was, I think, because he had misheard some wicked sect, which wrongly explained “Let there be light” (Genesis 1:3) as spoken by the Creator in the form of a wish, that he said: “For the Creator certainly did not borrow light from above, like people who light their lamps from their neighbours.” And it was because he had misheard another, impious sect that he also said this: “If the one who made these things against the great God’s will was some accursed god opposed to him, why did he lend him the light?”

We are so far from having to defend ourselves against these charges that we want to accuse those people’s opinion of error more plainly still, and take our stand not, as Celsus does, against what we do not know of theirs, but against what we know accurately: partly from the people themselves, whom we have followed closely, and partly from careful reading of their writings.

choices.choice: Origen refers to his own earlier discussion of the six days (generally identified with his lost Commentary on Genesis); the bracketed [τῶν] of the edition is not translated. ‘The word promises the righteous through Isaiah’: ὁ λόγος could mean the scriptural word or the divine Word speaking through the prophet; kept lowercase because the referent is not certain. Isaiah 60:19 LXX reads ἔσται σοι κύριος φῶς αἰώνιον καὶ ὁ θεὸς δόξα σου; Origen recasts it in the third person plural (αὐτοῖς, αὐτῶν), so ‘their’ stands outside the quotation marks. ἐχρήσατο is taken as the aorist middle of κίχρημι (‘borrowed’), matching ἐκίχρα (‘lent’) in the next quotation. In ‘why did he lend him the light?’ the subject is the great God; the Greek leaves it unexpressed and so does the English. ‘An accursed god’: lowercase because Celsus is describing the inferior Creator-god of the sect’s scheme. πῇ μὲν ἀπ᾿ αὐτῶν, ἀκολουθήσαντες: the comma in the transmitted punctuation is awkward; taken as ‘partly from the people themselves, having followed them closely’.
‘will live in a condition of day’ → ‘will be in a state of day’ (ἐν καταστάσει ἔσεσθαι; ‘live’ was added)
Celsus’s second quotation reordered so παρὰ γνώμην τὴν ἐκείνου goes with ‘made these things’ and τις is kept (‘some accursed god opposed to him’); dropped the added ‘acting’
‘we would rather accuse’ → ‘we want to accuse’ (ἐθέλειν)
Isaiah 60:19 and Genesis 1:3 checked against the LXX; correct

anf_compare.notes: Crombie (ANF 1872) and Chadwick (1953) were not used or consulted; the English is from the Greek.
